title: Little Venice, little Sparta: The UAE’s statecraft meets the war on Iran – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Cinzia Bianco argues the UAE's connectivity model (hub to every great power, backed by an interventionist military) survived the 2026 US-Israel war on Iran, but Iran's 3,000+ projectiles on Emirati ports, airports, data centres and energy sites showed entanglement does not buy protection; Abu Dhabi is moving toward 'fortified connectivity' (spare capacity, Hormuz bypasses, sovereign defence production) amid an open rupture with Saudi Arabia. Europe should leverage its role as endpoint, regulator and security partner via an EU-UAE Strategic Partnership Agreement, infrastructure protection and red lines on weaponised connectivity. (Text is internally inconsistent on OPEC exit timing: once 'OPEC+ in 2025', once 'OPEC this year'.)

themes.theme: Iran war stress test of the hub model

insights.claim: The UAE's assumption that commercial entanglement with Iran under a US deterrence umbrella would keep regional conflict away failed: Iran struck Emirati ports, energy sites and financial infrastructure anyway.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Gulf-hub risk premium must now price direct attack risk on commercial infrastructure.
insights.quote: Despite deep economic ties with the UAE, Iran struck Emirati ports, energy sites and financial infrastructure, showing that entanglement does not guarantee protection.

insights.claim: By April 2026 Iran had aimed more than 3,000 projectiles at Emirati bases, Dubai and Abu Dhabi airports, Jebel Ali and Fujairah ports, hotels, commercial data centres and oil/gas facilities such as Habshan and Ruwais.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Gulf data-centre, port and energy assets are proven targets, relevant to AI infrastructure siting.
insights.quote: By April 2026, Iran had aimed more than 3,000 projectiles at Emirati military bases

insights.claim: Traffic through Emirati ports including energy exports nearly halted; Fujairah, the only UAE export terminal outside Hormuz, became the lifeline and was repeatedly attacked.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Even bypass terminals are vulnerable; Gulf export capacity can drop near zero in war.

insights.claim: Before the war the UAE was Iran's largest import source and third-largest export market, and an FT analysis found 22% of 1,573 US-sanctioned Iran-linked entities based outside Iran had a UAE address, second only to China.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE financial channels are central to sanctions enforcement; elevated compliance risk for UAE-exposed banks.
insights.quote: 22% of 1,573 Iran-linked entities and individuals sanctioned by the US Treasury and based outside Iran had a UAE address
insights.locator: Where the connectivity strategy did not

insights.claim: On August 18th the UAE suspended all commercial and financial exchanges with Iran, and the next day Trump warned any country giving Iran 'any type of lifeline' would face severe consequences.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Secondary-sanctions threat raises risk for any Iran-linked trade flows globally.
insights.locator: So Abu Dhabi tried to manage

insights.claim: The UAE still keeps some channels to Iran open, calculating this is the best way to prevent Tehran and allies treating Emirati infrastructure as a pressure point, as they did to Saudi Arabia in September.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Abu Dhabi's hedging may spare its infrastructure relative to Saudi assets.
insights.locator: So Abu Dhabi tried to manage

insights.claim: The war exposed the limits of outsourced deterrence: Israel would not win the conflict on the UAE's behalf, the US launched the war without a plan to contain Iranian retaliation, and China did nothing to protect shipping and joined Russia in vetoing a Hormuz navigation resolution.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Gulf states will self-insure via defence spending and diversified partners.

insights.claim: Abu Dhabi's likely response is 'fortified connectivity': keeping the global-hub role while adding spare capacity, alternative routes, sovereign tech capabilities and indigenous defence production.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Capex wave in Gulf logistics redundancy and local defence manufacturing.
insights.quote: in which openness to global flows is backed by spare capacity, alternative routes, sovereign technological capabilities and increasingly sophisticated indigenous defence production

insights.claim: If Iran treats Hormuz hegemony as spoils of war, the UAE would pursue 'zero Hormuz' dependency by expanding Fujairah, Dibba, Rugaylat and Khorfakkan, deepening rail and pipelines, or even building a canal to the Arabian Sea.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Major infrastructure opportunities in Gulf of Oman ports, pipelines and rail.
insights.locator: Three lessons followed for Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Lessons include that military deterrence cannot substitute for a regional political arrangement limiting attacks on commercial assets, and that AI data centres may need to be put underground.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Hardening adds cost to Gulf AI data-centre buildouts.
insights.locator: Three lessons followed for Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: The UAE aims to cash out the oil era while it lasts and position itself in post-oil power industries like advanced manufacturing, technology and AI.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Sovereign capital will keep flowing into AI and advanced manufacturing.

insights.claim: Every additional node in the network creates a new target, and fortification can provoke counter-coalitions against the UAE.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Fortified connectivity carries escalating geopolitical risk, not just resilience.
insights.quote: they cannot eliminate the underlying problem that every additional node also creates a new target an adversary can threaten

insights.claim: Network centrality can compensate for smallness but cannot abolish geography, give a middle power a veto over great powers, or substitute for credible defence and a regional security order.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Limits of middle-power hedging strategies in a polarising world.

insights.claim: Longstanding UAE-Saudi differences hardened into an open rupture, with Riyadh now contesting Emirati influence directly; Vision 2030 megaprojects like NEOM compete for trade and capital that flowed through Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Gulf hub competition affects regional HQ, logistics and capital allocation.

insights.claim: The UAE left OPEC (the text also says OPEC+ in 2025), escaping Saudi-set quotas and gaining room to fund its plans.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE outside quotas implies higher potential supply and weaker OPEC cohesion.

insights.claim: Since the Iran war began Abu Dhabi has moved toward defiance and forceful deterrence while Riyadh prioritises restraint and a negotiated settlement.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Divergent Gulf war postures complicate any GCC-wide response.

insights.claim: Israel has largely displaced Saudi Arabia as the UAE's 'strategic multiplier', delivering air defence and counter-drone capabilities during the Iran war when Arab and Gulf partners did not.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE-Israel defence-tech cooperation will deepen.

insights.claim: Saudi officials believed the UAE brokered Somaliland's normalisation with Israel in exchange for Israeli security access to Berbera.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Red Sea basing competition is intensifying.
insights.locator: The UAE’s defiance is showing up

insights.claim: The UAE fears the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan could encircle it, but Egypt and Turkey depend too much on Emirati money to join an anti-UAE bloc.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Economic leverage limits formation of hostile coalitions.
insights.quote: each depends too much on the UAE economically to become a reliable member of a coalition against it
insights.locator: Both countries show how the UAE’s

insights.claim: The Houthis have pursued control of Mokha port and Perim island, which would let them close Bab al-Mandab as Iran did Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Red Sea shipping closure risk compounds the Hormuz disruption.
insights.locator: A foothold in the Red Sea

insights.claim: In 2025 the UAE announced a 10-year, $1.4trn US investment framework spanning critical minerals, AI infrastructure, semiconductors, quantum and biotech, with the relationship shifting from procurement to co-production.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Large sovereign capital flows into US strategic tech sectors.
insights.quote: in 2025 Abu Dhabi announced a 10-year, $1.4trn investment framework

insights.claim: China became the UAE's largest trading partner by 2020, with bilateral trade above $95bn in 2023 and over 15,000 Chinese firms in the UAE; about 60% of Chinese exports to the region reportedly passed through UAE ports.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE remains the gateway for Chinese trade into the Middle East.

insights.claim: The UAE treats IMEC and China's BRI as additive: better to be a node on every corridor than a partner in one.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE logistics assets benefit from any corridor that wins.
insights.quote: better to be a node on every corridor than a partner in one

insights.claim: The US stalled F-35 sales to the UAE in 2021 over Chinese technology exposure, leading Abu Dhabi to conclude a bipolar order offers it nothing and to favour a multipolar framework.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: US-China tech rivalry constrains Gulf access to US advanced tech.

insights.claim: DP World operated in 78 countries in 2024 and AD Ports had 33 terminals in more than 50 countries; DP World took a 30-year Tartus concession (Nov 2025) and AD Ports agreed a 20% stake in Latakia's container terminal (May 2026) alongside CMA CGM.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Emirati port operators are building Mediterranean/Red Sea corridor footholds, including in Syria.
insights.locator: Syria is where such a corridor

insights.claim: The UAE agreed with Jordan in 2024 to build a 360km railway to Aqaba with plans to extend it through Syria to the Mediterranean.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Overland Red Sea-Mediterranean corridor reduces Suez reliance.
insights.locator: Ultimately, the UAE wants to operate

insights.claim: Emirati entities have announced more than $168bn of African investment since 2017, Dubai hosts over 30,000 African companies and is the main market for African gold, with more than $1bn of Sudanese gold passing through the UAE in 2025.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: UAE is a key node in African minerals and gold supply chains, with sanctions/ESG exposure.

insights.claim: UAE microchip exports to Russia rose fifteenfold in 2022 to $24.3m, prompting Western warnings that the UAE was a transshipment hub for Russian tech procurement.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Export-control enforcement risk on UAE re-exports.

insights.claim: Ukraine gained new value for Abu Dhabi because its military has the deepest battlefield experience against Iranian-designed Shahed drones; a UAE-Ukraine 10-year drone deal was signed in 2026.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Counter-drone tech demand from Gulf buyers; Ukrainian defence-tech export opportunity.
insights.locator: The Iran war strained that relationship

insights.claim: The EU is the UAE's principal regional commercial partner with €55bn goods and €39bn services trade annually; the UAE broke GCC ranks to pursue a bilateral CEPA with Brussels, launched in May, irking Riyadh.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: EU-UAE trade deal could open market access ahead of a GCC-wide deal.

insights.claim: Europe's leverage stems from being the endpoint of Emirati supply chains, a regulator (CBAM on aluminium and steel, the AI Act) and a security partner; the UAE prefers adaptation over confrontation, as shown by exiting FATF and EU money-laundering watchlists by 2025.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: EU regulation shapes Emirati aluminium, steel and AI export economics.
insights.locator: Finally, Abu Dhabi treats its relationship

insights.claim: Europe should make the EU-UAE Strategic Partnership Agreement the backbone of ties, concluded before October 2029, including an EU-UAE-Ukraine counter-drone production compact.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Possible joint-financed counter-drone production lines involving European industry.

insights.claim: European naval missions in the Gulf and Red Sea are fragmented, under-resourced and mandated only to protect shipping; one should be extended to cover ports and undersea cables.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Undersea cable and port protection may become funded EU missions.

insights.claim: The UAE allegedly pressed London in 2024 to stay silent on intelligence tying it to Sudan's RSF and in 2015 dangled a $9bn arms contract to push a Muslim Brotherhood crackdown, illustrating post-Brexit Britain's vulnerability to Gulf capital leverage.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Gulf investment into the UK carries political strings.

insights.claim: Europe should tie expanded defence-industrial and technology access to benchmarks such as ending support to militias like the RSF, and coordinate red lines so Abu Dhabi cannot play capitals off each other.
insights.speaker: Cinzia Bianco
insights.so_what: Conditionality could slow some EU-UAE defence and tech deals.
insights.locator: In the military sector in particular
